title: What's new with the F1 Sprint in 2027?
excerpt:
The 2027 Formula 1 calendar is out and, among other things, you will have noticed there are more Sprints than ever before. Here's what you need to know...

How many more Sprints are we talking and why are we increasing?

The Sprint has been a hit and so due to the increasing popularity of the format, there'll be four more than in 2026, bringing the overall total to 10.

Since the Sprint concept was introduced in 2021, data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends.

Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than practice (Sprint Qualifying replaces second practice on a Friday afternoon on non-Sprint weekends).

Meanwhile, 82% of attendees at Sprint weekends say it adds value to their ticket with competitive sessions taking place on three days, rather than two on a traditional weekend.

Data also shows 75% of F1 fans believe Sprint events add greater value to a season’s calendar.

As a result, the number of Sprints has risen from three each year in 2021 and 2022 to six each year between 2023 and 2026 with 10 planned for next season.

Gotcha. Will any venues get a Sprint for the first time?

Yes – Bahrain, which hosts the season opener, Australia, Japan, Monaco plus the season finale in Abu Dhabi will all get their first taste of the Sprint format.

Sorry, did you say Monaco is getting a Sprint?

Yep, you read that right. One of the most exhilarating sessions to watch in Formula 1 is Qualifying in Monaco as drivers navigate the tight and twisty streets of Monte Carlo.

Now, fans will get to enjoy not one but two of those spectacular sessions in the Principality.

Sprint Qualifying will take place on Friday ahead of the Sprint on Saturday morning (which replaces FP3) and then Qualifying for the main Grand Prix takes place later on Saturday.

Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season with 10 Sprint events

Okay, so you've mentioned five of the Sprints – what about the other five?

Canada will host a Sprint for the second successive year, with Mercedes duo George Russell and Kimi Antonelli having delivered a sensational battle for the lead there earlier this year.

Silverstone gets its third Sprint after hosting one in 2021 and earlier this year, while Monza gets its second Sprint, six years after the Temple of Speed hosted its first.

Brazil extends its record of having hosted the most Sprints as it returns for the sixth edition at the iconic Interlagos track in Sao Paulo.

Qatar is back with a Sprint too, with Lusail getting a fourth one in five years.

With Abu Dhabi also hosting one, the season will end with back-to-back Sprints, leaving more points available for the final two Grands Prix weekends of the year.

At the other end of the calendar, with Bahrain, Australia and Japan hosting their first Sprints, it sees the season start with three Sprints in the first four race weekends – and that will reward teams who are fast and competitive straight out of the box.

Great stuff. Just remind me about the format of a Sprint?

Of course! As the name suggests, it's a short race. It runs over 100km, which is around one-third of a typical Grand Prix distance. It lasts roughly 30 minutes.

There are no mandatory pit stops like the Grand Prix and, while they are not banned, given the Sprint is so short it's not worth boxing for fresh rubber.

Points are awarded for the top eight positions with eight for the winner down to one for P8.

The introduction of the Sprint means the number of practice sessions are reduced from three one-hour sessions to just one 60-minute run.

Sprint Qualifying is a shortened version of the main Qualifying session, with SQ1 running for 12 minutes, SQ2 for 10 minutes and SQ3 for just eight minutes.

All in all, it means more competitive sessions across a season.

title: Everything you need to know about the 2027 F1 calendar
excerpt:
The 2027 Formula 1 calendar is out – and you'll find familiar faces, returning venues and more Sprints than ever before. Here's everything you need to know...

Okay, you've got my attention. What lies in store next year?

We've got 24 Grands Prix on the cards with Bahrain hosting the season-opener as part of a double header with Saudi Arabia in March.

The teams and drivers will then embark on a global odyssey across five continents, visiting historic venues and major global destinations before arriving at the finale in Abu Dhabi in December.

The calendar runs across 10 months and was created with sustainability in mind, with races grouped together to allow for an efficient geographical flow of events across the year.

And for 2027, as the Sprint format has proved so popular, the championship will raise the number of race weekends that feature a Sprint from six to 10. More on that later.

I can't wait. What's the plan after the initial Middle Eastern double header?

Australia, which hosted this year's opener, moves to race three and is the start of a triple header with Japan (don't worry, it'll still be cherry blossom season when we hit Suzuka) and China.

Then there's a move to North America for the first of three visits to the United States with the Miami Grand Prix.

There's a two-weekend gap before the Canadian Grand Prix with freight going direct to Montreal.

Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season

Nice! When do we get to Europe, then?

That's the next stop! Monaco remains in its new June date and opens the European leg of the season, with Portugal returning to the calendar after signing a two-year deal.

The Autodromo Internacional do Algarve (most commonly referred to as Portimão) is located in Portugal's southernmost region and hosted F1 in 2020 and 2021 during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The 4.6km circuit is an absolute corker as it delivers a technical challenge across dramatic elevation changes amid surrounding historic charm and spectacular beaches.

Oooooh, sounds lovely. Then it must be time for Silverstone?

You guessed right. Silverstone swaps places with Austria to form a double before another double in Belgium and Hungary.

The championship then breaks for the summer for some well-deserved time-off for racing personnel.

We're back in September at Monza, with the Italian race at the historic Temple of Speed forming a double header with Spain's Madring, which will host its second-ever Formula 1 race weekend.

What about the other returning race?

That'll be Türkiye, which makes a return to Formula 1 in the middle of an entertaining triple header with Azerbaijan and Singapore.

The Turkish Grand Prix was last staged in 2020 and 2021, with Lewis Hamilton securing his seventh Drivers' Championship at the venue at Istanbul Park.

The race signed a five-year deal through the 2031 season and is home to the very cool multi-apex Turn 8 that tests a driver's precision and commitment through its long, sweeping left-hander.

Great stuff. Then how does the end of the year look?

It's reassuringly familiar with Austin heading a triple header with Mexico City and Brazil's Sao Paulo before F1 makes its third and final stop in the United States with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

A Middle Eastern double header in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in December then closes us out.

Domenicali reflects on 'fascinating' season so far

Tasty. The 2027 season can't come soon enough!

We're with you! As I teased earlier, you'll get more qualifying and racing than ever before as the championship is increasing the number of Sprint events from six to 10.

Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco and Abu Dhabi will host the format for the first time. And Canada, Great Britain, Italy, Brazil and Qatar will get another shot to host a Sprint.

You can read more about the Sprint format and plan for next year here.

This is music to our ears. Just one last question - what's the plan for testing?

I’m glad you asked. With new regulations being introduced this year, teams had a five-day Shakedown in Barcelona followed by two three-day tests in Bahrain to prepare for the season.

With continuity in the rules heading into 2027, pre-season testing is reduced to one test, lasting four days in Bahrain at the Bahrain International Circuit at the end of February.

title: Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season
excerpt:
Formula 1 and the FIA have announced, following approval by the World Motor Sport Council, the 2027 FIA Formula One World Championship calendar, featuring 24 Grands Prix across 22 countries and 10 Sprint events.

Pre-season testing will take place in Bahrain from 24–27 February before the Championship returns there for the first race, followed by Saudi Arabia. The calendar then moves to Australia, Japan, and China, followed by the Miami and Canadian Grands Prix.

The European leg includes Formula 1’s return to Portugal in June, after Monaco, with Türkiye rejoining the calendar in October between Azerbaijan and Singapore. The closing phase of the season features races in Austin, Mexico City, Sao Paulo and Las Vegas, before the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Bringing together historic venues and major global destinations across five continents, the 2027 calendar reflects Formula 1’s continued growth as a global sport and entertainment platform while supporting its long-term sustainability goals through a more efficient geographical flow of events across the season.

Due to the continued success and strong demand for the format, the number of Sprint events has increased from six to 10 for 2027, delivering even more competitive action across the season for fans, promoters, broadcasters, and partners. Since the Sprint was introduced in 2021, the data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends. Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than Free Practice, 82% of attendees at Sprint weekends say it adds value to their ticket, and 75% of F1 fans believe Sprint events add greater value to a season’s calendar.

Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco, and Abu Dhabi will host Sprint events for the first time, with fans set to enjoy two thrilling qualifying sessions in Monaco as the drivers show their world class skill and precision on the narrow streets of Monte Carlo. Sprint events will also return to Montreal, Silverstone, Monza, Sao Paulo and Lusail creating even more action-packed race weekends for audiences around the world.

The full 2027 F1 calendar can be viewed below:

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1, said: “The 2027 calendar brings together some of the most iconic circuits and vibrant cities in the world, creating an incredible stage for another unforgettable season of Formula 1. We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Türkiye to the championship and to expand Sprint racing to ten events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special.

"Formula 1 continues to go from strength-to-strength, attracting new audiences around the globe. Week after week, the world's greatest drivers will battle on some of the most challenging tracks in motorsport, supported by F1’s outstanding teams, world-class manufacturers, and global partners.

"Together, they create a spectacle unlike anything else in sport. As we continue this remarkable journey of growth, I want to thank our fans around the world as their passion drives everything we do.

"I want to thank The President of the FIA, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, and the FIA, our teams and drivers, promoters, partners, sponsors, and host cities for their continued commitment and support and we recognise the extraordinary dedication of the volunteers, marshals, and officials whose hard work makes every Grand Prix possible.

"We are incredibly excited to see this calendar come to life and to deliver another season packed with unforgettable moments, fierce competition, and world-class entertainment for our fans across the globe.”

Everything you need to know about the 2027 Formula 1 calendar

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, added: “The 2027 FIA Formula One World Championship calendar is a strong reflection of the global appeal and continued growth of our sport.

"With 24 Grands Prix across five continents, the return of Portugal and Türkiye, and the opportunity for an expanded Sprint programme, the calendar combines tradition, innovation, and fan engagement while maintaining the highest sporting standards.

“I would like to thank Formula One Management, the promoters, the national sporting authorities, the FIA officials and volunteers and all our stakeholders for their collaboration and commitment.

"Together, we continue to strengthen the FIA Formula One World Championship and deliver an exceptional season for competitors and fans around the world.”

title: 'McLaren’s call to pit Norris after the VSC made no sense'
excerpt:
Lando Norris and McLaren were left despondent after a race that looked to be theirs got away in Madrid. For the second time in seven days Kimi Antonelli benefitted from a Virtual Safety Car and in Spain he snaffled the win away from a driver who did everything right.

McLaren were desperately unlucky with the timing of the VSC. They missed out on both ends of it by small margins. Lance Stroll’s car was stationary for a full 30 seconds before the VSC was deployed, after he was forced to stop on track with a mechanical problem on his Aston Martin.

title: Victoria Farfus sets the pace in 2026 F1 ACADEMY Rookie Test
excerpt:
Victoria Farfus topped the timesheets as F1 ACADEMY concluded its 2026 Rookie Test at the Circuito de Navarra.

Designed to give up-and-coming young female drivers the chance to demonstrate their potential for a future full-time seat or Wild Card opportunity on a level playing field, the second edition of the Rookie Test featured an expanded format.

Last month’s Rookie Training Camp at Loughborough University saw the field undertake a range of physical and cognitive assessments alongside interactive workshops to accelerate their development on and off the track.

Following the camp, the drivers gained insights into the demands of competing in the series, immersing themselves within the six F1 ACADEMY teams during the 2026 field’s two days of in-season testing and participated in assessment activities.

The Rookie Test concluded with one day of on-track action. The 18 drivers representing 14 countries got behind the wheel of the F1 ACADEMY machinery, completing 1,447 laps across the board. Farfus secured the fastest overall time, the 15-year-old Brazilian posting a 1:46.988 to finish three tenths clear of Sofia Zanfari and Rosanne Den Drijver in the morning segment.

The afternoon running saw Alexia Danielsson top the timesheets, recording a 1:47.259 in the McLaren OXAGON-liveried car, beating Ella Lähdemaa and Farfus by two tenths. The Rookie Test also featured familiar names such as former 2026 Wild Cards Autumn Fisher and Zoe Florescu, alongside Mercedes junior Luna Fluxa Cross.

The success of the Rookie Test has already been seen, with seven drivers graduating to full-time seats following the inaugural event including Zandvoort Reverse Grid Race winner Payton Westcott and podium finishers Megan Bruce and Natalia Granada.

Katie Denver, Performance & Talent Development Manager, F1 ACADEMY said: “The Rookie Test has been a fantastic opportunity for the rookies to showcase their potential and benchmark themselves against other aspiring drivers and the current F1 ACADEMY grid.

“It has also provided valuable insight into the strengths, development areas and future potential of the next generation of female racing talent. The preparation and commitment shown by all participating drivers throughout the test has been impressive, and we look forward to following their continued progression.”

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Madrid?
excerpt:
Victory went to Kimi Antonelli at the Spanish Grand Prix after the timing of the Virtual Safety Car scuppered Lando Norris’ efforts. But who impressed our Power Rankings judges over the course of the weekend at the all-new Madring? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Norris appeared to do everything right last weekend, bouncing back from technical troubles during Friday practice to take a superb pole position and then surging into a comfortable lead in the early stages of the race. However, a Virtual Safety Car came out at just the wrong time (after he had passed the pit entry) and left him having to settle for P3. Our judges were nonetheless clear on who deserved to top the rankings.

Antonelli was the big beneficiary from Norris’ misfortune – pitting under the VSC himself and taking the lead when Norris stopped. The young Italian continued to impress, however, by comfortably leading the Mercedes charge and ultimately extending his championship lead over team mate George Russell to 81 points.

Max Verstappen gave little away about his and Red Bull’s hopes after a low-key Friday practice in Madrid, but both driver and team stepped forward in Qualifying to come away with a very solid third on the grid. That became second in the race due to Norris’ VSC drama, and a fifth podium finish in the last seven events. “The car is the car, and I think for us to be second is a very good result,” he summed up afterwards.

Franco Colapinto is enjoying a much stronger run at Alpine in 2026, with the Argentinian growing in confidence as he builds experience in the top echelon. The last two events have been particularly encouraging – back-to-back Q3 spots and points being achieved at Monza and in Madrid. After turning ninth on the grid into seventh at the chequered flag on Sunday, he described “probably my best race weekend” in the sport.

Arvid Lindblad looked rapid during Friday practice at Madring, before pushing too hard on a soft-tyre run in FP2 and slamming into the barriers. He rebuilt his confidence, though, to make it through to Q3 and bag more points – his ninth score in the last 10 weekends. Our judges continue to be impressed by the sport’s latest rookie driver.

Battling with Lindblad in the closing stages of Sunday’s race was Nico Hulkenberg, who just missed out on a spot in the final shootout in Qualifying, before edging himself into points contention during a long, hot race in the Spanish capital and coming away with 10th – the German’s third top-10 finish in four events.

While Antonelli and Verstappen pitted under the VSC, and Norris stopped just after it ended, Charles Leclerc extended his opening stint and waited it out for a potential Safety Car. That never came, leaving the Monegasque fourth at the finish, but feeling that there was not much more on the table for himself and Ferrari.

Leclerc was the sole Ferrari driver to make the flag at the Madring after Lewis Hamilton’s early retirement due to brake problems. Hamilton had looked quick in final practice, only to find the wall at the final corner, then led the first Q3 runs before winding up fourth. “I think we had the car to fight for a win today, and unfortunately it just didn’t work out,” he said in the media pen.

After a difficult mid-season run, Esteban Ocon enjoyed a stronger weekend at the Spanish Grand Prix. He was quick in Friday practice, placed 13th in Qualifying and ended the race just outside the points in 11th – while team mate Ollie Bearman got stuck at the back of the field following his heavy crash in FP3 and pit lane start.

Liam Lawson was given a third weekend in the Red Bull in Madrid as Isack Hadjar continues his recovery from a wrist injury. He lacked some confidence during Friday practice but qualified a respectable eighth (not a world away from Verstappen’s lap time) and went on to finish the race in sixth, for his best result at the senior team.

Missing out

Just missing out on a spot in this week’s Power Rankings list is Russell, who started the weekend by topping FP1 but lost confidence as the track conditions improved – meaning he had to settle for sixth in Qualifying and fifth in the Grand Prix.

title: How Sainz’s home race in Madrid unravelled
excerpt:
If there was one weekend this year where Carlos Sainz was hoping that better Williams form and perhaps some attrition ahead would combine to propel him up the order it was always going to be his home race in Madrid.

Unfortunately, while the local hero received huge support, the new track did not favour the Williams FW48 from the start of practice on the car’s final outing before the Baku upgrade package arrives.

Things began to fall apart for Sainz in Qualifying, and then a first lap incident scuppered any chance of making progress. And it didn’t go much better for his Williams team mate Alex Albon.

The pair qualified in P16 and P17, with Albon ahead, and the fact that they were split by just 0.005s in Q1 suggested that both men had found the limit of the car.

It then got worse for Sainz as he received a three-place grid penalty for impeding Valtteri Bottas that sent him down to P20, behind the two Cadillacs.

Wary of how hard overtaking was expected to be, Sainz went for it at the start and he paid the price when he made contact with the Racing Bulls of Yuki Tsunoda at Turn 1, picking up some floor damage in the process.

"I had a really good start off the line,” he said. “I think I got three or four positions on the hard tyre, and then a lot of bunching up into Turn 1 caught me a bit out, and I had a small contact with Tsunoda that damaged my floor.

“Unfortunately from there on, I had damage in the car, and it was a race of survival, because I had no rear downforce in the car for the rest of the race.

“So yeah, we had nothing to lose on that Lap 1, and I wanted to get a good start to see if we could get anything going in this race.”

A little later Sainz got into another scrape at Turn 5, this time with his countryman Fernando Alonso, who felt he was squeezed.

Having damaged his front wing Alonso made his feelings about the incident clear on team radio, and just for good measure he reminded the world – and the stewards – of Sainz’s first corner mishap.

“Nothing to say really,” Sainz noted. “It's the nature of that corner when you turn right, and I think he complained on the radio, so he managed to get me a penalty, like always. I think it's the nature of that corner, it's always going to lead to these kinds of crashes, because there's only space for one.

“There's not even space for two. So yeah, and you cannot keep looking in your mirror while you're turning, and doing a right/left because you need to look forward. So at one point you need to focus on your own driving line, and I don't think Fernando was alongside me or anything.”

Sainz took a five-second penalty at his pit stop. Given the floor damage and the impact on performance the team eventually decided that it wasn’t worth continuing, and the car was retired after 43 laps.

“Just there was no downforce in the car,” he said. “So I was just driving around one second off the pace with the floor damage. It was slight damage, honestly, it wasn't that big of a contact, but with these cars, the moment you lose a piece of the floor, it's game over.”

He added: “But in reality, even with a perfect race, we wouldn't have finished higher than 16th. So yeah, not a lot to fight for today.”

It was not what Sainz wanted for his home town race, but on the plus side he at least enjoyed the love that he received from the crowd.

“Honestly, it was an amazing weekend on that front,” he said. “I truly enjoyed seeing the support that we got from all the fans. Their behaviour, the support that I've caught this weekend is second to none, and I cannot thank them enough for making me feel so at home in my home.

“And I’m looking forward already to next year. As I said in many interviews, hopefully this is the last year here in Madrid that I'm fighting for P16, and from next year onwards I can fight for something more, because honestly, it's not ideal to be fighting at home for a P15, P16 all weekend.”

Meanwhile it was an equally frustrating Sunday in Madrid for Albon, who ended up in the better of those two positions. However he struggled for pace throughout, coming under pressure from Cadillac’s Sergio Perez.

“I think one of my stronger weekends, but at the same time, just super, super sketchy,” said Albon. “Realistically, the pace isn't quick enough, and I think, especially on the harder tyres, we don't have the load to keep the tyre alive. So that tyre has actually got very little degradation, but it just cools down once the tread comes off the tyre.

“You need to keep pushing on it to keep the temps up. We don't have the grip to do it. Just the tyres get cold, basically.”

title: Tsunoda reviews Madrid outing after sustaining 'big damage'
excerpt:
Yuki Tsunoda endured a race to forget in Madrid, as the Racing Bulls stand-in finished down in 14th on a day that could end up being his final Formula 1 start.

After being hit by Carlos Sainz at the first corner, he was left driving a damaged Racing Bulls car and thus never had a chance to make any progress.

The Madring was Tsunoda’s third outing as replacement for Liam Lawson, who in turn was drafted into Red Bull to deputise for the injured Isack Hadjar.

Tsunoda put himself back on the F1 radar with a solid P11 in the Dutch GP, and by subsequently scoring a point with P10 at Monza.

Another good run in Madrid would have further strengthened his case to return to a race seat in the future and it looked good on Friday when he finished FP2 in eighth, his team mate Arvid Lindblad having demonstrated the potential of the VCARB 03 with P4 before his big crash.

However, when it mattered in Qualifying on Saturday things drifted away from Tsunoda and he could qualify only P15.

“Yesterday, I knew there are a lot of places I can improve, from the car and everything,” he said after the session. “Something didn't really click today. Just pace was not there at all.

“Somehow, just it degs a little bit in terms of car pace. I just didn't feel any tyre grip, even sometimes it felt old tyres were better than new tyres. Something felt very odd, so I have to find out why. In general, I just didn't have grip.”

That misfortune continued into Tsunoda’s race day, which was compromised from the start when he was hit hard on the left side by Sainz.

Not only did he lose spots to Alex Albon and Sergio Perez, but he also sustained damage that made it even harder for him to find a way past the Cadillac driver.

“Pretty much the race was finished by that,” he said after the flag. “I lost a lot of positions by that, but also I had a big damage from that. Honestly, it was very difficult to overtake here, even though I had a still good advantage to the car in front in terms of pace. But just a really pressurising race, honestly.”

While the Racing Bulls had the potential to be faster than Perez, there was nothing that Tsunoda could do. However, when Perez pitted under the VSC, Tsunoda was able to find some performance.

“I mean, suddenly the car got cleared in front, and the pace suddenly recovered a lot. And to be honest, considering that damage I had, the pace wasn't that bad. But yeah, it was super difficult to overtake here.”

At the chequered flag he was in P14, which was not what he wanted on a day when Lindblad finished P9.

“In general there's something this week that wasn't easy at all,” he said. “And being unable to, I would say, solve the issue that I had since FP1, probably for me that issue got worse and worse throughout the week. So yeah, something to review. I mean, in the race, nothing I can do.”

title: Mekies assesses Lawson's Red Bull stint after Madrid
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies has praised Liam Lawson's "very strong" stint with Red Bull, with the New Zealander standing in for the injured Isack Hadjar across the last three race weekends.

Lawson's promotion back to Red Bull, albeit on a temporary basis, has been a chance of redemption after the 24-year-old managed just two race weekends for the team at the start of the 2025 season before being sent back to Racing Bulls.

His latest stint with the senior squad has been much more positive with seventh on his first outing in Zandvoort, while he backed that up with a solid sixth last weekend in Madrid.

With plenty more experience under his belt, Red Bull team boss Mekies has been impressed with what Lawson has managed to achieve so far.

“I think he's done a very good job," he said. "I think we all know how difficult it is to jump to a different team, to a different car, and I think that he has done that to the best of what could have been our expectations.

“He has taken some very important points today with the P6. He did the same in Zandvoort and in Monza he would have done something similar without the contact with Nico [Hulkenberg] and the front wing damage.

“So, I think he did a very good job, again very different pictures compared to the first two races of 2025 when he was in the team so we are thankful and happy with that.”

During his brief stint with Red Bull at the start of 2025, Lawson qualified 18th and 20th in his two qualifying sessions with the team and he was also 20th on the grid for the first Sprint of the season. He failed to score in either Australia or China, in stark contrast to team mate Max Verstappen who finished those races second and fourth.

But thus far, his second Red Bull stint has been much more positive. He has qualified eighth twice in the two race weekends where his performance was unhampered by grid penalties – Lawson was forced to take a grid drop at Monza as his car needed a raft of new PU components, which understandably hindered his race performance.

Having finished seventh and sixth in Zandvoort and Madrid, he has added to the team’s points tally, and has also been respectable in terms of pace difference to Verstappen. Jumping into the car at a Sprint weekend, while also having to drive the RB22 at a new track, also meant the timing was less than ideal for the New Zealander.

But a year and a half’s worth of added experience seems to have very much paid off this time around.

“I think he has continued to grow as a driver and he's very calm in the car, he is very focused,” added Mekies. “He's certainly making - I don't know if he makes an effort or not - but he's certainly managed to keep things simple in the way he interacts with the team and in the way he tackles his own performance and the car performance.

“So, he's focused on the essentials. He tries to get the basic rights and it's working for him, of course with more time in the car, you can then get to another degree of finesse, maybe. But I think that approach is very, very strong.”

Whether Lawson gets a fourth go at Red Bull remains to be seen, with Hadjar still recovering from the wrist injury he sustained in the summer break.

title: LIVE: Max Verstappen vs 100
excerpt:
Max Verstappen faces arguably his most unusual challenge yet this evening as he lines up last on a 101-kart grid at Silverstone, tasked with overtaking all 100 drivers ahead of him within 30 laps.

The Red Bull star will start from P101 on a purpose-built kart circuit, with identical machinery for every competitor.

The 100 challengers, a mix of athletes, content creators and fans, will do everything they can to keep Verstappen behind.

Each driver he passes is eliminated, but there is a twist: the challengers can each use a track shortcut once in the first 15 laps, while Verstappen can only deploy his after half distance.

The win condition is simple but brutal: pass all 100 or fail. The race gets underway at 6pm.

title: Haas facing final evaluation as 2027 line-up decision nears
excerpt:
The Haas F1 team will carry out a test later this week as it closes in on a decision over its driver line-up for the 2027 season.

While Oliver Bearman is widely expected to continue with Haas for a third-straight season, the identity of his team-mate has not yet been confirmed.

Currently in the second seat is Esteban Ocon, who joined the American squad last year following a stint at Alpine.

As the team mulls over its options, fresh contenders have emerged - including Formula 2 championship contender Rafael Camara.

It has been rumoured that Camara is in the strongest position of all contenders to obtain a seat and step up to F1 as a rookie driver next year.

However, RacingNews365 understands that no such decision will be made until after Haas conducts a TPC (testing of previous cars) run at Jerez later this week.

On Thursday, Jack Doohan will get behind the wheel as the team evaluates his potential for a promotion next year.

Doohan has seven grand prix starts in his career with Alpine, but was dropped from a race seat shortly after the start of 2025 campaign in favour of Franco Colapinto.

At the start of 2026, Doohan joined Haas as a reserve driver in a bid to get himself back onto the grid.

While it seems Camara is in the better position as things stand, it is a challenging decision for the team to make, as his promotion would see Haas field two Ferrari juniors.

It is understood would bring some financial backing to Haas, but the team would effectively be without its own in-house competitor, with Ferrari having ultimate control over their futures.

Finally, one outside option for Haas is its development driver, Ryo Hirakawa.

The Japanese driver has taken part in multiple FP1 outings with Haas over the last two years as part of the team's relationship with Toyota Gazoo Racing.

However, paddock voices suggest that Hirakawa's chances are minimal at best.

title: Cadillac deliver Sergio Perez response after 'disappointment' verdict
excerpt:
Sergio Perez recently voiced his disappointment with the form on display from the Cadillac team.

16 September 5:15PM

Cadillac team principal Marcin Budkowski has issued a response to Sergio Perez after the Mexican voiced “disappointment” over the squad's form.

The American outfit joined the grid as an 11th team this year and immediately placed at the back of the field as it got up to speed in the sport.

Following a difficult period in recent events, Perez has stated there has been “a lot of disappointment” within the team due to the lack of progress.

But Budkowski, who took over at the helm of the team from Graeme Lowdon midway through the campaign, stated he informed Perez that he needed to keep his expectations in check.

When asked by media including RacingNews365 if the team has reached a development plateau, Budkowski said: “No.

“I think you have to put that in perspective with the drivers’ expectations and the reality of the seasonality of F1.

“Before I even started, after my appointment was announced, I had a quick chat with both drivers.

“And Sergio asked me, 'What are you going to do for Zandvoort?', which is a week after I started. And I said, 'Well, Checo, I think I need to control the expectations a little bit.'”

Cadillac has switched focus to 2027 F1 car

While Cadillac has been located at the back of the field thus far, it has also battled several reliability issues, particularly regarding its brakes.

Addressing its struggling form, Budkowski detailed that Cadillac's performance has taken a knock due to applying resources to fix such concerns, as well focus now being switched to the 2027 challenger.

“The reality is we’re in a phase of the season where we’re all working on next year’s car,” he said.

“We’ve switched the resources mostly to next year. We have a development pipeline that’s slowly drying out.

“A lot of our resources have also been, unfortunately, busy fixing our reliability issues rather than working on performance items. So naturally, the development is plateauing in this phase of the season.

“But I think on our side, we have a lot of potential through fixing the reliability, fixing the operational side, fixing the quality of the car.

“There’s performance there that we can still extract this year. But our focus needs to be on next year’s car, and I think everybody will tell you this up and down the pit lane.”

title: Aston Martin fear 'dramatic' unthinkable over Fernando Alonso
excerpt:
Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack believes it would be “unthinkable” and "dramatic" if Fernando Alonso opted to quit the team and F1 at the end of this season.

Alonso is weighing up his future at a time when Aston Martin is suffering on track after a major change to this year's regulations, and also in taking on a new power unit partner after joining forces with Honda and ending its prior partnership with Mercedes.

The two-time F1 champion has made clear he will not be rushed into making a decision, primarily as he waits to see if the team can continue to make gains over the remainder of the season after taking a step in the right direction recently. Honda, however, is still struggling.

Krack can appreciate why Alonso is biding his time.

"At the end of the day, we have always been clear that the team wants to continue [with him], but we need to respect what Fernando's thoughts are and the time he wants to take," he said, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"As I've said before, we're confident we can reach a good solution for everybody. Now it's about waiting. He needs to make up his mind, and then we move on."

Alonso has additionally made clear his dislike of the regulations, describing F1 as "a battery world championship".

Last weekend in Madrid, the new home of the Spanish Grand Prix, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has stated that he plans to talk with Alonso to convince him to stay, and that he should not end his remarkable F1 career with a season like this.

"He has made clear that it is not one single thing that he wants to see change," said Krack. "And yeah, I read about these discussions [with Ben Sulayem] as well. The sport needs someone like that.

"We will all be keen to see Fernando continue. What can be done to accommodate, I think, it will be done, and then I hope we can come to a good solution and continue."

[Article continues below]

Aston Martin refusing to discuss 'plan B'

At this stage, Krack is refusing to divulge whether the team has contingency plans should Alonso opt to quit, believing it has time on its side.

"I will not give you any names [of a potential replacement], and I will also not speak about any plan B," he said.

"We very much hope that Fernando will continue. He's very important for our team, very important for Formula 1, and motorsport in general."

As to the alternative, however, that is a possibility Krack does not want to consider.

"It would be a pity to not have him anymore," he said.

"And because that would be so dramatic, I do not even want to talk about it or think about it."

title: Max Verstappen predicts 'carnage' at unique Red Bull outing

Max Verstappen is taking part in a unique event today with Red Bull, facing 100 opponents at Silverstone!

Max Verstappen is expecting to see “carnage” unfold at Red Bull's karting event at Silverstone, where he will attempt to overtake 100 opponents.

“I haven’t driven in go karting in quite a few years so it will be fun to go back and see how I go, but there are a lot of people to overtake so let’s see!"

title: Max Verstappen, Lando Norris, and Fernando Alonso clear crucial Le Mans F1 roadblock
excerpt:
Could we see an active F1 driver return to the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2027? It is certainly possible?

Max Verstappen, Lando Norris, and Fernando Alonso could all potentially race at the 2027 Le Mans 24 Hours after a crucial roadblock was avoided.

The twice-around-the-clock French endurance race is scheduled for June 12th-13th, 2027, and falls within a gap in the 2027 F1 calendar, which was unveiled on Wednesday morning.

The Monaco Grand Prix takes place on Sunday, June 6th, before the returning Portuguese Grand Prix at Portimao is pencilled in for Sunday, June 20th.

It means the weekend of June 12th-13th is free and a clash with Le Mans, as happened in 2026 for the first time since 2016, is avoided.

Alonso is the only one of the trio to have competed at Le Mans, winning for Toyota in both 2018 and 2019, the former when he was an active F1 driver for McLaren - the last driver to compete at the Circuit de la Sarthe whilst being active in grand prix racing.

Norris has recently tested McLaren's new Hypercar at Portimao as McLaren prepare to enter the class next year, with Verstappen long stating his ambition to race at Le Mans.

Qualifying and practice takes place the week of the race, meaning there would not be a clash with F1 duties, whilst the rookie orientation test must also be completed.

The article continues below.

Not the only clash avoided

An F1 grand prix also clashed with the other race in motorsport's 'triple crown' in 2026, with the Canadian GP over-lapping the the thrilling photo-finish of the Indianapolis 500.

For 2027, another clash has been avoided.

The trip to Montreal ends with the grand prix on Sunday, May 23rd, with the Indy 500 taking place on May 30th.

This then leads into Monaco on June 6th, before Le Mans on June 12th-13th.

However, it would not be possible for any driver to compete in all three 'Triple Crown' races, as the numerous practice sessions and qualifying for the Indy 500 clash directly with F1's Canada weekend.

2027 F1 pre-season testing dates

F1 has confirmed the dates for its sole pre-season test in 2027 ahead of a record-breaking schedule.

The new 2027 calendar was unveiled on Wednesday featuring 24 races and a record 10 Sprints, including in the Bahrain opener, the Abu Dhabi finale, and most eye-catchingly of all, at the Monaco Grand Prix in June.

Testing has usually been held at the circuit since moving from Barcelona, with Bahrain offering teams stable conditions in which to put their new cars through their paces, unlike the uncertainty of the middle of the European winter, with snow falling on occasion in Spain.

It means teams will come from the Milan season launch between February 18th and 20th before heading to Sakhir, which will also host the season-opener on March 14th, with it being one of the 10 Sprint events.

However, there is the possibility of testing and the first race, being moved away from Bahrain, owing to the uncertainties in the Middle East as the Iran War continues.

F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali has previously stated that a decision on whether the 2027 season can start in Bahrain is required to be taken by the end of the 2026 calendar year.

title: Five big takeaways from F1's eye-catching 2027 calendar reveal
excerpt:
RacingNews365 takes a look at five of the most eye-catching stories in the 2027 F1 calendar.

The 2027 F1 calendar is finally here.

Announced by the championship on Wednesday morning, it features 24 grands prix, beginning on March 14th in Bahrain and concluding in Abu Dhabi on December 12th.

You can check out the full calendar by clicking this link.

Below, RacingNews365 takes a look at five of the most eye-catching aspects to the new schedule.

1. A Sprint race in Monaco

Perhaps the most eye-catching detail in the calendar announcement was the fact that, for the first time, a Sprint will be held at the Monaco Grand Prix.

On the surface, this appears to be a strange decision given the lack of overtaking in the Principality over the years and calls to shake-up the format, including the doomed mandatory two-stop rule for the 2025 race.

Qualifying is often deemed the highlight of the Monaco weekend, and so F1 will be doubling up on the action that is one of the great spectacles in motorsport.

It means practice will be shaved from three hours to just one before Sprint Qualifying, perhaps throwing extra jeopardy into the weekend.

2. The number of Sprints

Including Monaco, there will be a total of 10 Sprints on the 2027 calendar, a rise of four from 2026, which featured six.

It is a climb of seven from the format's first season in 2021, which offer a total of 80 championship points, over three grands prix worth.

A total of six of the 10 will be in the first half of the season before the summer break, in Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Canada, Monaco, and Great Britain.

The remaining four will be in Italy, Brazil, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi. It means that for the first time, the season-finale will be a Sprint weekend, with three of the final four featuring the format, at a time when the championships will be decided.

F1 has made clear that viewing figures and interactions of the Sprints have been steadily increasing, so the format is firmly here to stay and could yet expand further in the future.

3. The start could yet change

The season-opener is currently pencilled in for Bahrain on March 14th, with Saudi Arabia following a week later in a double-header.

However, given the uncertainty in the Middle East regarding the ongoing Iran War, a question mark must be placed over these two grands prix opening the 2027 season.

Should the need arise for the races to be moved backwards, Australia will not fill in as the season-opener, with it being understood that a start at the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai is being considered with the Japanese GP also moving forward, in a possible direct swap with Bahrain and Saudi Arabia.

F1 boss Stefano Domenicali has previously stated that a decision on whether the 2027 season can begin in the Middle East must be taken by the end of the 2026 calendar year at the latest, owing to logistics.

4. Bi-annual rotation begins

F1 has previously had rotation between grands prix, most famously the German GP between Hockenheim and the Nurburgring between 2008 and 2014, before Hockenheim continued in even-numbered years until '18, with a one-off event in '19.

But it has become a rarity in recent years, but given the boom in countries interested in hosting, bi-annual rotation has become the solution to too many races and not enough slots on the calendar.

For 2027, this begins with the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix dropping off as it begins its even-numbered run, with the Belgian Grand Prix at Spa featuring in odd-numbered years until 2031.

Elsewhere, the Dutch GP has fallen off the calendar after its contract expired, with the Portuguese and Turkish GPs returning, having both last featured in the 2021 season as COVID replacements for the long-haul flyaways.

5. No clashes with Le Mans or Indianapolis 500

In 2026, the start of the Canadian Grand Prix overlapped directly with the thrilling photo-finish of the Indianapolis 500, whilst the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix was a clash with the end of the Le Mans 24 Hours.

Fortunately, for 2027, no clash between either of the races happens with an F1 race.

The Canadian GP takes place on May 23rd, before Indianapolis on May 30th.

Monaco follows on June 6th before Le Mans on June 13th.

It means the likes of Lando Norris, who has recently tested McLaren's Hypercar, Max Verstappen, and two-time Le Mans winner Fernando Alonso, could, hypothetically, compete at the twice-around-the-clock French test of endurance.

title: FIA president points to 'strong appeal' behind record-breaking F1 calendar

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has spoken of the continued "strong global appeal" of F1 after the 2027 calendar was dropped.

title: F1 CEO promises 'more intensity' as major calendar decision made
excerpt:
F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali has promised fans "more intensity and drama" after the 2027 calendar expanded the number of Sprints to 10.

The 2027 schedule dropped on Wednesday morning, with the championship featuring 10 Sprints dotted throughout the season, a rise from six in 2026.

Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Canada, Monaco, Great Britain, Italy, Brazil, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi will all feature the shorter race, with the season-opener and season-finale in Bahrain and Abu Dhabi, respectively, hosting Sprints for the first time.

Most eye-catchingly, Monaco will also host a Sprint for the first time, with six being held in the first 12 races, and four in the second 12 of a 24-grand prix schedule, including three of the final four races.

Speaking about the new schedule - available to view here - Domenicali spoke of the promise of more of the "wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special."

"The 2027 calendar brings together some of the most iconic circuits and vibrant cities in the world, creating an incredible stage for another unforgettable season of Formula 1," said Domenicali.

"We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Turkey to the championship and to expand Sprint racing to ten events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special.

"Formula 1 continues to go from strength to strength, attracting new audiences around the globe. Week after week, the world's greatest drivers will battle on some of the most challenging tracks in motorsport, supported by F1’s outstanding teams, world-class manufacturers, and global partners.

"Together, they create a spectacle unlike anything else in sport. As we continue this remarkable journey of growth, I want to thank our fans around the world, as their passion drives everything we do."

The article continues below.

Domenicali issues thanks

Domenicali also offered his thanks to his FIA counterpart Mohammed Ben Sulayem, and the thousands of others who make an F1 season possible.

"I want to thank the President of the FIA, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, and the FIA, our teams and drivers, promoters, partners, sponsors, and host cities for their continued commitment and support," he said.

"And we recognise the extraordinary dedication of the volunteers, marshals, and officials whose hard work makes every grand prix possible.

"We are incredibly excited to see this calendar come to life and to deliver another season packed with unforgettable moments, fierce competition, and world-class entertainment for our fans across the globe."

title: F1 unveil 2027 season calendar with record number of Sprints
excerpt:
2027 F1 season calendar unveiled

Formula 1 has unveiled its 2027 race season calendar, featuring 24 grands prix - and a record number of 10 Sprint races.

The 2027 campaign is due to begin in Bahrain on March 14th and conclude in Abu Dhabi on December 12th, with both the Portuguese and Turkish Grands Prix returning to the schedule on June 20th and October 3rd, respectively.

With Portugal and Turkey returning, the Barcelona-Catalunya and Dutch Grands Prix have fallen off for 2027, as Barcelona enters a bi-annual rotation with Belgium starting from 2027.

The season is set to be supplemented by a record-breaking 10 Sprint events, with the Monaco Grand Prix across the first weekend in June set to feature the second race for the first time. For the first time, the season finale in Abu Dhabi will also feature the shorter race format, with six Sprints in the first 12 races and four in the second-half of the season.

There is still uncertainty whether the proposed calendar will be followed, owing to the ongoing Iran War that has seen the 2026 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix postponed whilst the Bahrain GP was rearranged for Malaysia.

F1 has still not confirmed whether the 2026 Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix will go ahead in November and December of this year, but it is increasingly likely that they do not, with Imola understood to be stepping in as the season finale on December 6th.

F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali had previously indicated that the middle of September was when the championship required a decision on those two races, owing to freight logistics, and that a decision on whether Bahrain and Saudi Arabia could host early 2027 season races would not need to be formally made until the end of the 2026 calendar year.

title: Isack Hadjar lengthy injury absence defended as Liam Lawson again waits
excerpt:
The French driver has now missed the last three grands prix following his over-aggressive training workout during the summer break.

16 September 10:15AM

Nico Rosberg has defended Isack Hadjar in light of the Red Bull driver coming under fire for his lengthy absence following a wrist injury over the F1 summer break.

Whilst boxing training, it is understood that Red Bull driver Hadjar fractured his wrist punching a heavy bag in the gym.

The injury has forced the Frenchman to miss the last three grands prix in the Netherlands, Italy, and most recently, the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, with Liam Lawson deputising on each occasion.

Speaking on Sky Sports F1 during the Madring weekend, Rosberg pushed back on criticism of the 21-year-old, drawing a comparison with Lance Stroll's 2023 pre-season cycling accident.

"It's really horrible to drive with a wrist injury," said Rosberg.

"We've seen Lance Stroll do that a few years ago, incredibly, and because of the G-forces and everything, it's so extreme.

"And especially, what you don't really think about is when you're braking, you fly forwards in the seat belts, and you have to push against the steering wheel because otherwise your body just flies forwards, and you wouldn't want to hang in the seat belt like that.

"So you're pushing very hard against the steering wheel, which, if your wrist is broken, you can't do that; you'll be in too much pain."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Isack Hadjar

French

6

The Stroll precedent

Stroll fractured both wrists, along with a partial fracture to his left hand and a broken toe, after crashing during road cycling training in Spain in February 2023. He still raced two weeks later at the Bahrain Grand Prix, finishing sixth.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has insisted there is no cause for alarm over Hadjar's recovery, stating the timeline remains normal for the injury he sustained.

"There is nothing wrong with Isack's recovery," said Mekies. "We will evaluate the situation in a week... to put him on the simulator, to expose him to real-life constraints.

"If he feels close to 100 per cent, we go for it; if he feels the recovery is not completed, we will stick to our approach to put his recovery first."

Lawson, who has covered for Hadjar throughout the layoff, conceded the uncertainty around his own role for Baku is taking a toll.

"It's possible the decision about which car I'll drive in Baku won't be made until Wednesday or Thursday," he said.

"It's psychologically challenging to prepare when you still don't know what car you'll be driving. The more I drive this car, the more comfortable I feel, and going back to another one will be difficult."

title: Lando Norris reveals 'easy changes' after 'useless' quip
excerpt:
The F1 champion feels there are possibilities to turn the Madring into an exciting racing circuit.

16 September 9:30AM

Lando Norris feels there are "easy changes" that could be made to the Madring after slating it as a race track, deriding one section in particular as "useless".

After finishing third in Sunday's inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the circuit in the north-east of Spanish capital, Madrid, Norris pulled no punches in his condemnation of a venue that just 24 hours previously had yielded a spectacular qualifying session.

The concern going into the race, however, was the quality of actual racing that would be delivered, and so it proved, as there were apparently just four overtakes throughout after the usual opening-lap skirmishes.

The main target of Norris' ire was a section of the circuit in the final sector.

"There are some obvious changes they should make," said Norris, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "They should get rid of 18, 19. Useless! Just have more of a straight into a hairpin.

"I don't know how someone looks at this design [in planning] and goes, 'Mint'."

The 26-year-old, who had claimed pole position on Saturday with a lap described as "a masterpiece" by team principal Andrea Stella, said the circuit still had potential if organisers acted on his suggestions.

"There's a lot of opportunity," he said. "I think they can make it into a track that's good for racing, and I'm excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes because I think it's a track that is good fun to drive. It can be a great racetrack."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lando Norris

British

1

Norris makes Austin comparison

Norris' call for changes was echoed throughout the paddock, including by those on the podium with the Briton in Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, who extended his lead at the top of the drivers' standings to 81 points with his victory, and four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen.

Several other drivers, including Oliver Bearman and George Russell, also identified the combined braking and turning zone around Turn 5 and Turn 6 as a fundamental flaw that made defending too simple and overtaking nearly impossible.

Antonelli and Verstappen reportedly agreed that a complex chicane section like Turns 5-6 carried too great a risk of contact and wall strikes rather than encouraging clean racing.

Making clear that, as it stands now, Madring is "not a great racetrack", he added: "It's great in qualifying, but [let's have a] straight line from 17 straight to 20, have a much wider entry like Austin Turn 1 or Turn 10 in Austin, big hairpin. You'll create much better opportunities for everyone, and you'll be able to enjoy the race."

Norris acknowledged that not every problem area was as straightforward to solve, singling out the Turn 5, 6 and 7 sequence as a tougher puzzle for designers.

Even so, he was adamant that most of the fixes needed at Madring were well within reach for organisers before the circuit returns to the calendar.

"There are some simple changes, and maybe some trickier ones, like Turns 5, 6, 7," he said. "It's hard to know exactly what's the best thing.

"But the fact you have to turn and brake basically defeats the whole object of racing. They can do some simple changes, easy changes, and maybe some more tricky, but I hope they do it."
